text.p: Haralambros Papadias, the first Greek to win a global sprint title, has been spared potential embarrassment by the world governing body when he steps forward to claim his $50,000 prize money.
Papadias won the world indoor 60 metres title here on Friday at the first world championships in which prize money will be awarded to medal winners.
According to International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) rules, all athletes eligible for prize money must have undergone two out-of-competition tests.
Papadias could prove he had passed only one random test but the IAAF decided a test conducted on the first day of the championships on Friday would also count.

The 22-year-old Greek, whose best for the 100 metres is only 10.27 seconds, is among a group of Greek athletes being investigated by the IAAF after their coach clashed with a dope tester in Germany last month.
"He was in that group in Dortmund but we don't know if he was in the stadium or his hotel or another site," IAAF spokesman Giorgio Reineri said on Saturday.
"We don't know if anyone tried to stop him."
German tester Klaus Wengoborski has alleged he was pushed by an angry Greek coach when he was trying to carry out random doping tests in Dortmund.
Wengoborski also said the Greek athletes left the stadium before he was able to test them.
Reineri said the "story was very near to being clarified".
The IAAF doping commission will make a report to the IAAF Council at a meeting in Turin later this month, he said.
The commission asked for reports from the German tester and the Greek federation after the Dortmund incident.
World record holder Emma George of Australia soared over the bar to qualify easily for the women's world pole vault final after some confusion over the qualifying height.
George said she did not know whether or not she had to vault 4.10 metres but decided to attempt the height anyway.
Asked if she would break her own world record of 4.55 metres the former trapeze artist in a troupe rejoicing in the name of the "Flying Fruit Fly Circus" replied: "I hope so."
She then added: "I have just come here to win, I would have come anyway."
Lebanese high jumper Jean-Claude Rabbath was taken to hospital after crashing against the upright bar in the men's high jump qualifying.
A statement from the organisers said Rabbath had sustained a neck injury but added "there did not seem to be any heavy neurological signs".
